Kth Largest Element in an Array
O(n log k). Quickselect averages O(n).
Merge K Sorted Lists
O(N log k), where N is the total number of nodes
Find the Median from a Data Stream
Implement a Min-Heap from scratch (array-based)

A complete binary tree stored in an array. push and pop are O(log n), peek O(1). Building a heap from n items with bottom-up sift-down is O(n), not O(n log n). Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default; use Comparator.reverseOrder() for a max-heap.
K Closest Points to the Origin

To keep the k smallest, use a max-heap of size k (and vice versa). O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Compare squared distances to avoid sqrt, and use Integer.compare rather than subtraction to avoid overflow. Quickselect gives O(n) average.
Kth Largest Element in a Stream
Keep only the k largest values seen so far in a min-heap; its root is the answer. Each add is O(log k) and memory stays O(k) however long the stream is.
Last Stone Weight
A straightforward max-heap simulation: repeatedly take the two largest. O(n log n).
Top K Frequent Words (ties broken alphabetically)
The size-k min-heap must evict the "worst" word, so the tie-breaker is reversed inside the heap and the result is reversed at the end. O(n log k). Getting the comparator right is the real test here.
Reorganize String (no two adjacent characters equal)

Always place the most frequent remaining character, but hold it out of the heap for one step so it cannot repeat. It is impossible when any count exceeds (n + 1) / 2. O(n log 26) = O(n). Task Scheduler uses the same idea with a cooldown of n.
Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix

Treat each sorted row as a list and do a K-way merge, exactly like Merge K Sorted Lists: O(k log n). An alternative is binary search on the value range, counting elements ≤ mid with a staircase walk: O(n log(max − min)).
Kth largest: sort vs heap of size k vs quickselect

| Sort | Min-heap of size k | Quickselect
Time | O(n log n) | O(n log k) | O(n) average, O(n²) worst
Extra space | O(log n) for int[] | O(k) | O(1) iterative
Streaming input | No | Yes | No (needs all data)
Modifies input | Yes | No | Yes (partitions in place)
Gives the top k in order | Yes | After polling, O(k log k) | No, only partitioned
Rule of thumb: heap of size k is the safe default and works on streams. Quickselect is the "can you do better?" answer; use a random pivot.
Top K: min-heap of size k vs max-heap of all n elements

| Min-heap, keep size k | Max-heap of everything, poll k times
Time | O(n log k) | O(n) build + O(k log n)
Space | O(k) | O(n)
Head of heap is | The k-th largest (the weakest kept) | The largest
Works on a stream | Yes | No
Rule of thumb: for the k largest keep a min-heap (so the smallest of the kept ones gets evicted); for the k smallest keep a max-heap. The heap type is the opposite of what the name suggests.
PriorityQueue vs TreeSet / TreeMap as a priority structure

| PriorityQueue | TreeSet / TreeMap
Peek min | O(1) | O(log n) (first())
Peek max as well | No | Yes (last())
Remove an arbitrary element | O(n) | O(log n)
Duplicates | Allowed | Set drops them; use TreeMap<value, count> or add a tie-breaker
Iteration order | Not sorted | Sorted
Rule of thumb: only need the top → PriorityQueue. Need both ends, or to delete specific items (sliding window median, order books) → TreeMap with counts, or lazy deletion in two heaps.
Building a heap: n offers vs heapify (PriorityQueue(Collection))

| n × offer() | Heapify (sift down from n/2 - 1 to 0)
Time | O(n log n) | O(n)
Java | for (x : list) pq.offer(x) | new PriorityQueue<>(collection)
Why the difference | Each insert may climb the full height | Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a little
Comparator | Any | The Collection constructor uses natural order (or a SortedSet / PQ's comparator)
Interview tip: "building a heap is O(n)" is a classic follow-up. Heapsort uses it: O(n) build, then n pops at O(log n).
